fixture.description: v2's twelve reads, unchanged, plus the write half of the same loop. The reads are the contract section 1 and 6 second baseline: same twelve reads, same order, same pinned ids, same frozen board. The writes are the four board writes around one unit of work, measured as one `transact` and as four separate commands, always against a per-iteration disposable copy of the frozen fixture.

writes.description: The write half of one agent-loop iteration: the four board writes a /kb worker issues around one unit of work - claim, checkpoint under that lease, progress note, release - measured two ways. `transact_items` is the whole unit as ONE `kanban transact` (kanban 2815693, ADR-041), threading the lease with a `$ref` instead of a round trip. `per_command` is the same four commands one at a time, threading the token by hand, which is what the deployed loop does today. Both run against a per-iteration disposable copy of the frozen fixture; see `scratch`.

placeholders.TASK: the claimed task id, chosen at run time by `task_selection`; never hardcoded, because a frozen id may already be claimed or done
placeholders.TOKEN: the lease token `claim` answered with, substituted by the driver only in `per_command`; inside `transact_items` the same value travels as a `$ref` and never leaves the host

task_selection.pick: the first candidate whose status is todo; `claim --candidates` already excludes rows with unmet dependencies and rows someone holds
task_selection.run: once per run, over one cold ssh, against a throwaway scratch copy that is removed immediately afterwards - not against the frozen fixture, and not inside any measured window
task_selection.on_empty: the run FAILS LOUDLY: no candidate means there is nothing this fixture can claim, and a write half with no task is not a measurement. The driver aborts the write half, records the refusal in `writes.error`, and exits non-zero.

writes.provenance_note: The checkpoint carries --repo/--branch/--head/--dirty explicitly. ADR-008 (rust/lib.rs:3576) refuses a checkpoint whose provenance would be blank, and captures it from the caller's git checkout otherwise: an `ssh host kb ...` lands in $HOME, so capture would either fail or record whatever checkout happens to be there. Explicit values make the write identical on every arm and on every host. --head must be at least 7 hex characters and --dirty must read like git status, so the values here are the kanban commit this fixture was written against and `clean`.

readback.run: after the measured window, over one cold ssh that reads the state and then removes the scratch copy; excluded from write_loop_ms
readback.equivalence: The write half is comparable iff every arm leaves the same projected state - same status, the claim gone, the same note count and the same checkpoint count - on every iteration. Counts are absolute rather than deltas because every iteration starts from a fresh copy of the same frozen board, so the baseline is a constant.

scratch.rule: NO ARM EVER WRITES THE FROZEN FIXTURE. Per iteration, per arm: `mktemp -d` on the remote, `cp -r /root/bench-fixture/. $scratch/`, `chmod -R u+w $scratch`, run the write half against the copy, read the state back, `rm -rf $scratch`. The copy and the removal are measured separately and are EXCLUDED from write_loop_ms; the copy is reported as scratch_copy_ms.
scratch.cleanup: rm -rf "$scratch", guarded by the /tmp/kb-bench-scratch- prefix so a blank or unexpected path is refused rather than removed
scratch.board_selector: --db $scratch/boards/<board file>, the copy's own board file. The basename is discovered at run time from the frozen registry (`workspace list --json`, already in the remote probe) and never hardcoded.
scratch.why_db_and_not_project: registry.db stores ABSOLUTE board paths, so the copied registry still names /root/bench-fixture's board: `--project kanban` under KANBAN_DATA_DIR=$scratch would open the FROZEN 0400 file and the write would either fail or, worse, land on the fixture. `--db` addresses the copy itself. It also takes no data-root lock (rust/lock.rs:130-147 - a board outside the data root is not data-root state), so a per-iteration temp directory needs no registry surgery.
scratch.data_root: Every arm inherits the kb-bench wrapper's default data root (/root/bench-fixture) and uses it for exactly one thing: the read-only registry lookup that resolves rule summaries. KANBAN_DATA_DIR is deliberately NOT overridden per iteration, because it could not be: an MCP arm is ONE persistent `ssh host kb mcp` child whose environment is fixed when the session opens, so a per-iteration data root cannot reach it while a per-iteration `--db` reaches every arm identically. Addressing beats environment here, and identical addressing across arms is what makes the arms comparable.
scratch.frozen_proof: The frozen board's size and mtime are probed before and after every write arm; a change disqualifies the receipt.
scratch.aux_transport: The copy, the readback and the removal always travel over their own cold ssh (ControlMaster=no ControlPath=none), on every arm including the MCP ones, so no arm's own channel is charged with the scratch lifecycle and no arm's reuse proof counts a request it did not make.

frozen_from.note: v2's `reads` carried over byte for byte - `diff <(jq -S .reads fixture-v2.json) <(jq -S .reads fixture-v3.json)` is empty, which is what keeps a v3 receipt's read numbers comparable with a v2 receipt's. This change adds only the `writes` section: the write half of the loop as one `kanban transact` (shipped at kanban 2815693, ADR-041) and as the same four commands one at a time. The write numbers have no earlier baseline; v3 is their first.

run.percentile_method: nearest-rank over successful measured loops: value at ceil(P/100*n), 1-indexed
run.timing: wall clock, time.perf_counter_ns on the client, per read and per loop. On mcp-batch a batched read's `ms` is the whole batch call's wall time attributed to that read, because one call has no per-read timing to observe; those per-read numbers therefore sum to far more than loop_ms and only loop_ms is comparable across arms. `write_loop_ms` is the write half's requests alone: the per-iteration scratch copy (`scratch_copy_ms`) and the readback that also removes it (`readback_ms`) are timed on their own cold ssh and excluded.
run.bytes: application-layer: request = the exec command string (ssh arms) or the JSON-RPC frame (mcp); response = stdout bytes (ssh arms) or the JSON-RPC frame (mcp); body_bytes = the kb --json output either way. On mcp-batch a batched read's request and response bytes are that entry's slice of the one frame, so they sum to the frame minus its envelope. On ssh-transact the request is the command string plus the item list it sent on stdin. Not wire bytes.

arms.description: one persistent `ssh <target> kb mcp` child; every batchable logical read of the loop is carried in a single `tools/call batch` per iteration, the rest issued as ordinary tools/call on the same pipe. Per-read `ms` for a batched read is the WHOLE batch's wall time attributed to that read: inside one call there is no per-read timing to observe, so those numbers sum to far more than `loop_ms` and only `loop_ms` is comparable. Per-read `bytes_sent`/`bytes_received` are that entry's slice of the request and response frames, so they sum to the frame minus its envelope rather than to a per-read frame.

transport.note: the -v flag is on the one long-lived ssh so its stderr proves a single authentication; -v prints nothing per tools/call. A batch carries only tools whose tools/list entry is readOnlyHint true, which is read off the server at setup rather than assumed here
transport.batch_tool: batch (rust/mcp.rs): up to 32 read-only tool calls per request, validated whole before any entry runs, results returned in order

setup.unbatchable_reason: the tool's tools/list entry is not readOnlyHint true, so `batch` refuses it; issued as its own tools/call on the same pipe
